edges.effect_quant: Coffee looks more promising for fatal prostate-cancer outcomes than for total prostate-cancer incidence, with dose-response syntheses suggesting a modest downward association.
edges.population: adult men with habitual coffee consumption
edges.mechanism: Coffee may influence insulin signaling, inflammation, and tumor-metabolic pathways in ways that matter more for progression and lethal disease than for initial diagnosis. That progression-focused mechanism fits the epidemiology better than a broad incidence-prevention story.
edges.summary: If coffee has a meaningful prostate-cancer signal, it probably shows up here rather than in total incidence. The strongest anchor is the dose-response meta-analysis linking higher intake to lower fatal prostate-cancer risk, and later cohort-only syntheses generally point the same way even when the overall disease picture stays mixed.
edges.caveats: Most of the evidence is observational and some analyses derive the mortality conclusion from subgroups rather than from a dedicated mortality-only literature. This is enough for a cautious protective edge, but not for a strong prevention claim.

evidence.citation: Discacciati A et al 2014 Ann Oncol
evidence.notes: Coffee consumption and risk of nonaggressive, aggressive and fatal prostate cancer--a dose-response meta-analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: fatal prostate cancer risk per 3 cups/day increment in coffee consumption

evidence.citation: Huang TB et al 2014 Int Urol Nephrol
evidence.notes: Coffee consumption and urologic cancer risk: a meta-analysis of cohort studies.

evidence.citation: Huang TB et al 2015 Nutr Cancer
evidence.notes: Coffee consumption and prostate cancer risk: a meta-analysis of cohort studies.

effect_quant.comparator: fatal prostate cancer for highest versus lowest coffee intake
